action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.

schema.name: SendFeedback
schema.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Build Journal Setup Instructions

The page provides setup guidance divided into two sections:

## For Students

Students should open Claude Code in their project folder and paste this instruction:

> "Follow the setup instructions at https://phcompeau.github.io/ProgrammingforScientists2026Undergrad/project/journal/ for my 02-120 build journal, then tell me what you did."

Key points include:
- All Claude Code sessions in the folder are automatically copied to a `journal/` subfolder
- Regular commits and pushes are required
- Repository collection occurs at 11:59 pm on checkpoint dates: October 30, November 10, November 20, and December 1
- By October 30, submit the repository link on Canvas and add GitHub user `phcompeau` as a collaborator if private

The journal contains only project-specific sessions and excludes passwords and API keys.

## For Claude (Setup Steps)

1. Download `save_journal.py` from the provided URL and save as `.claude/hooks/save_journal.py`
2. Merge hooks from `settings.json` into `.claude/settings.json` without removing existing content

5. Check journal files for sensitive information; redact if found
6. Commit and push with message "Set up build journal"
7. Inform the student and remind them of submission deadlines

# Build Journal Setup URLs and Instructions

**Exact URLs:**
- save_journal.py: `https://phcompeau.github.io/ProgrammingforScientists2026Undergrad/project/journal/save_journal.py`
- settings.json: `https://phcompeau.github.io/ProgrammingforScientists2026Undergrad/project/journal/settings.json`

**"For Claude" Steps (verbatim):**

"1. Download [save_journal.py](save_journal.py) from `https://phcompeau.github.io/ProgrammingforScientists2026Undergrad/project/journal/save_journal.py` and save it, unchanged, as `.claude/hooks/save_journal.py`.
2. Add the hooks in [settings.json](settings.json) (`https://phcompeau.github.io/ProgrammingforScientists2026Undergrad/project/journal/settings.json`) to the project's `.claude/settings.json`. If that file already exists, merge the `SessionStart` and `SessionEnd` entries into it without removing anything already there. Use `.claude/settings.json`, not `settings.local.json`, so that the hooks are committed with the repository.
3. Run the script once by hand from the project root (`python3 .claude/hooks/save_journal.py`, or `python` on Windows) and confirm that `journal/` now contains one or more `.jsonl` files.

Exit code 1
# Project concept (working draft)

Status: **draft, expected to change.** Nothing here is final. Every science claim
is unverified until it is checked against the paper and marked with its page.

Source: Hanahan, D. "Hallmarks of cancer—Then and now, and beyond."
*Cell* 189, 2254–2277 (2026).

Mission: convey the hallmarks paper clearly to the player. Every mechanic must
come from the paper. If a mechanic doesn't teach the science, it's cut or changed.

## Core model (decided 2026-10-06)

Reproduce Armitage & Doll (1954), *Br J Cancer* 8:1 (`papers/brjcancer 00386.pdf`,
notes in `papers/armitage-doll-1954-notes.md`). If a cell needs r rare changes in
order, cancer incidence at age t grows like t^(r−1), so log(rate) against log(age)
is a straight line with slope r − 1 (pp. 2, 10). Their Table I slopes are
4.97–6.48 (p. 4), which means about 6–7 changes.

The model is a simulated population whose cells pick up hits over a lifetime,
with sliders, not just the formula. Real data to compare against: CI5-XII
incidence, England 2013–2017 (`data/`).

Decided 2026-10-07:
- One simulation = one person, a grid of cells, year by year from birth to 85
  (the last CI5 age group).
- Store every simulated person in a table (e.g. age at cancer, or none), then
  group into five-year age groups and compute new cases ÷ people still
  cancer-free, the same kind of number as the paper and CI5.
- v1 is the simplest grid: independent cells collecting hits, checked against
  slope r − 1. Then build up: cells that divide (Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002),
  colon layout (Nicholson et al. 2018), maybe immune cells later. See
  `research/cell-rules-candidates.md`.

The scientific question is still to be worded by Cameron.

## Where I want to take it: the game interface

The game below is only a way to explore the model, never the project itself.

## The idea

A single-player game. The player is an oncologist fighting a "cancer boss"
across stages of one person's life. As the person ages, the boss gains more
hallmarks and the body's own defenses weaken.

## Decisions so far (2026-10-06, all open to change)

- **Player:** the oncologist. The body is an ally whose own defenses act on
  their own and weaken with age.
- **Boss:** pure evolution, with no scripted AI. Its "intelligence" comes only from
  mutation plus selection in a cell population. The game shows the player that
  nobody planned it.
- **Winning a level:** a cure (tumor gone) or control (tumor kept stable and small
  for long enough). This matches adaptive therapy.
- **Stages:** the person's age. Mutations pile up and immune defenses weaken
  with age.
- **Language:** not chosen yet; we'll pick whatever fits the game.

## Candidate mechanics (all unverified)

1. Hallmarks unlock as the boss evolves; the number grows with each age stage.
2. A hallmark codex: each new hallmark gets a plain-language card tied to the
   paper, and that knowledge is needed to beat the level.
3. Each hallmark is paired with a real treatment type. Check against Hanahan's
   figure matching hallmarks to drug types.
4. Biopsy and DNA investigation: tumors are many different groups of cells, and a
   biopsy sees only part of the tumor (incomplete information).
5. Metastasis drives travel: the invasion hallmark seeds other organs.
6. Resilience counter: pre-cancers the body stopped on its own.
7. Treatment resistance: maximum dose selects resistant cells (adaptive therapy).
8. One scientific engine; each level changes its settings. v1 has one organ and
   2 to 3 hallmarks.

## Candidate model checks

- No mutations: no cancer ever appears.
- One hit (r = 1) gives a flat rate; two hits (r = 2) give a rate that grows in a straight line with age.
- The simulated log-log slope equals r − 1.
- CI5 England slopes compared with Table I (4.97–6.48).
- Circumcision check (pp. 8, 12): risks 0.30, 0.77, 0.98, 1.00 from 1 − ((53 − T)/53)^6.
- Maximum constant dose leads to resistant takeover. Adaptive dosing delays it.
- Growth with all defenses off matches logistic growth worked out by hand.

## Course guideline check

Checked against `course/guidelines.md` (2026-10-06, updated after choosing Armitage & Doll).

| Requirement | Status |
|---|---|
| Own GitHub repo | Done |
| All work in Claude Code inside the repo | Starting now (start sessions from the repo folder) |
| Language | No rule stated; the app must run on the web with nothing to install |
| **"No video game" rule** | **Risk:** must be a model answering a question, with the game only as a way to explore it |
| Q1: a scientific question | **Gap:** core is Armitage & Doll; Cameron to word the question |
| Q2: a working model someone can explore, not one figure | Fits if the model comes first |
| Q3: at least one concrete check | Candidates listed above |
| Reproduce a published result (suggested) | Armitage & Doll 1954, Table I slopes (numbers checked against the PDF) |
| Paper and sources in the repo | Done: Armitage & Doll and Hanahan PDFs in `papers/` |
| Data in the repo before proposing | Done: CI5-XII in `data/`, source and terms in `data/README.md` |
| Smallest version first | v1 = one organ, 2 to 3 hallmarks |
| Proposal due Oct 7 | **Tomorrow** |

# Project guidelines (summary)

Summary of `Project Description F26.pdf` (02-120, Fall 2026). When in doubt, the
PDF is the source of truth.

## What is graded

The goal is learning, not the product: "whether your brain got bigger along the
way, whether you can defend what you built, whether you checked it to make sure
it's right, and whether you used AI to learn rather than to avoid learning."

| Component | Share |
|---|---|
| Proposal (one page, three questions) | 5% |
| Build journal (Claude Code logs + git history, four checkpoints) | 35% |
| TA check-in (15 min, Nov 4–13) | 5% |
| Final app and code (live on the web, with repo + README) | 10% |
| Video demo (5 min max, own voice) | 10% |
| Project assessment (closed, on paper, in class) | 35% |

## Hard rules

- A computational model of a real scientific phenomenon that answers the three
  questions. Suggested: reproduce a published result, then take it further.
- **Not accepted:** "A project with no scientific question, such as a video game
  or a dashboard." Also not accepted: reinventing a standard package, a chain of
  library calls, a project whose only check is that it runs.
- Proposal (one page max) answers:
  1. What is your scientific question?
  2. What will you build to answer it? (A working model someone can explore,
     not a single figure.)
  3. How will you check your model? (At least one concrete check: a published
     value, a case solvable by hand, or a behavior the science requires.)

  It also names the inspiring paper or phenomenon, any data, and where you want
  to take the paper.
- Any data must be downloaded and in the repo **at proposal time**.
- Final app deployed to the web, usable without installing anything. README
  explains what it does and how to run it. Video linked from README and site.

## Build journal (how to work)

- All project work happens in Claude Code inside the repo, including learning the
  science. Keep the paper and sources in the repo.
- Commit early and often, **with commit messages in your own words**.
- Graders look for: steady sessions across weeks; learning with AI (being taught,
  quizzed, explaining back, asking Claude to explain its code, debugging
  together); checking work (tests, comparing output to the proposal's check).
- Not graded: number or polish of prompts, how much code Claude wrote. Dead ends
  are fine.
- A course-provided command copies session logs into `journal/`. Only the repo is
  collected; personal content can be redacted first.

## Pitfalls named

- Data never arrives. Obscure papers (prefer an older, famous result). Scope too
  big: get the smallest version working and checked first.

## Dates (11:59 pm Eastern)

| Date | What |
|---|---|
| Wed Oct 7 | **Proposal due** |
| Fri Oct 9 | Staff feedback |
| Wed Oct 21 | Journal checkpoint 1; revised proposal if asked |
| Fri Oct 30 | Journal checkpoint 2; project office hours |
| Nov 4–13 | TA check-ins |
| Fri Nov 20 | Journal checkpoint 3; first version live on the web |
| Tue Dec 1 | Demo day; final app, code, video due |
| Thu Dec 3 | Project assessment, in class |

#####
SPATIAL GAMES SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
=========================================
Status: VERSION 1 DONE (2026-10-04). Live at https://spatial-game.vercel.app/
  Built: rules + update step (66 checks), image start (20 checks), grid with the
  paper's colors, Play/Pause/Step/Reset, b slider + presets, random / one-defector /
  your-image starts, cooperator % readout, explainer, mobile layout.
  Not built from this spec: grid-size choices (49/99/199) and a tests.html page
  (checks run with node instead: node rules.test.js, node image.test.js).
Created: 2026-10-04. Decisions from review added 2026-10-04.


GOAL
----
A webpage that teaches the Nowak-May spatial games model. It shows the grid
playing the game over time, with a short explanation (a tutorial we will write)
beside it and a few controls for the user. It lives at a link I can share with
friends. Vercel integration is coming soon.


THE MODEL
---------
1. Every square is either a cooperator (C) or a defector (D).

2. When two squares meet they play one round of the prisoner's dilemma.
   Payoff to the first square:

                       vs C     vs D
       I am C           1        0
       I am D           b        0

   - Two cooperators: each gets 1.
   - Defector meeting a cooperator: the defector gets b (b > 1, a parameter);
     the cooperator gets 0.
   - Two defectors: each gets 0.

3. Each square plays that round against its 8 neighbors and sums its points.
   A square does NOT play itself (no self-play).

4. Then every square, all at the same moment, looks at itself and its
   neighbors and copies the strategy of whoever scored highest.
   Then the whole thing repeats.

5. Ties: if the square itself is among the top scorers, it keeps its own
   strategy. Otherwise, if the tied top scorers have different strategies,
   the square becomes a cooperator (C wins ties). Explain this in the tutorial.

6. Edges do not wrap around. Squares on an edge or corner just have fewer
   neighbors (5 on an edge, 3 in a corner).


SETTINGS
--------
- b: slider from 1.00 to 3.00 in steps of 0.01, value shown as a number.
  A change takes effect on the next step.
  b has its own slider only; presets never change it.
  Note from the paper (p. 829): without self-play the "interesting" chaotic
  range is 8/5 < b < 5/3 (1.6 to 1.67), with cooperators near 0.299. (The
  paper's main figures use self-play, where it is 1.8 < b < 2.) Checked in our
  code 2026-10-04 on a random 99x99 start: b = 1.61-1.66 gives ~30% C with
  ~1,700 squares changing per step; b <= 1.59 settles near 75% C; b >= 1.67
  freezes near 7% C. Default b = 1.65.
- Starting position and grid size: the user can choose both. Defaults come
  from the paper. Starting-position presets (famous starts) only set up the
  grid; they do not touch b:
    * Random, 10% defectors, 200x200 (paper Fig. 1 and 2a).
    * Single defector in the center of a 99x99 grid of cooperators
      (paper Fig. 3, the "evolutionary kaleidoscope").
    * More presets to add as we find them (e.g. a small block of C in a sea
      of D).
- Grid size control: fixed choices 49x49, 99x99, 199x199. Each preset sets
  its default size (random start: 199, kaleidoscope: 99; the paper used 200
  for random, but odd sizes keep a true center square), and the user can
  change it after.
- Reset: makes a NEW random start (random grid, 10% defectors) at the
  current grid size.


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
1. All-C grid: an interior square scores 8, an edge square 5, a corner 3.
#####

Summary of `Project Description F26.pdf` (02-120, Fall 2026). When in doubt, the
PDF is the source of truth.

## What is graded

The goal is learning, not the product: "whether your brain got bigger along the
way, whether you can defend what you built, whether you checked it to make sure
it's right, and whether you used AI to learn rather than to avoid learning."

| Component | Share |
|---|---|
| Proposal (one page, three questions) | 5% |
| Build journal (Claude Code logs + git history, four checkpoints) | 35% |
| TA check-in (15 min, Nov 4–13) | 5% |
| Final app and code (live on the web, with repo + README) | 10% |
| Video demo (5 min max, own voice) | 10% |
| Project assessment (closed, on paper, in class) | 35% |

## Hard rules

- A computational model of a real scientific phenomenon that answers the three
  questions. Suggested: reproduce a published result, then take it further.
- **Not accepted:** "A project with no scientific question, such as a video game
  or a dashboard." Also not accepted: reinventing a standard package, a chain of
  library calls, a project whose only check is that it runs.
- Proposal (one page max) answers:
  1. What is your scientific question?
  2. What will you build to answer it? (A working model someone can explore,
     not a single figure.)
  3. How will you check your model? (At least one concrete check: a published
     value, a case solvable by hand, or a behavior the science requires.)

  It also names the inspiring paper or phenomenon, any data, and where you want
  to take the paper.
- Any data must be downloaded and in the repo **at proposal time**.
- Final app deployed to the web, usable without installing anything. README
  explains what it does and how to run it. Video linked from README and site.

## Build journal (how to work)

- All project work happens in Claude Code inside the repo, including learning the
  science. Keep the paper and sources in the repo.
- Commit early and often, **with commit messages in your own words**.
- Graders look for: steady sessions across weeks; learning with AI (being taught,
  quizzed, explaining back, asking Claude to explain its code, debugging
  together); checking work (tests, comparing output to the proposal's check).
- Not graded: number or polish of prompts, how much code Claude wrote. Dead ends
  are fine.
- A course-provided command copies session logs into `journal/`. Only the repo is
  collected; personal content can be redacted first.

## Pitfalls named

- Data never arrives. Obscure papers (prefer an older, famous result). Scope too
  big: get the smallest version working and checked first.

## Dates (11:59 pm Eastern)

| Date | What |
|---|---|
| Wed Oct 7 | **Proposal due** |
| Fri Oct 9 | Staff feedback |
| Wed Oct 21 | Journal checkpoint 1; revised proposal if asked |
| Fri Oct 30 | Journal checkpoint 2; project office hours |
| Nov 4–13 | TA check-ins |
| Fri Nov 20 | Journal checkpoint 3; first version live on the web |
| Tue Dec 1 | Demo day; final app, code, video due |
| Thu Dec 3 | Project assessment, in class |

#####
SPATIAL GAMES SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
=========================================
Status: VERSION 1 DONE (2026-10-04). Live at https://spatial-game.vercel.app/
  Built: rules + update step (66 checks), image start (20 checks), grid with the
  paper's colors, Play/Pause/Step/Reset, b slider + presets, random / one-defector /
  your-image starts, cooperator % readout, explainer, mobile layout.
  Not built from this spec: grid-size choices (49/99/199) and a tests.html page
  (checks run with node instead: node rules.test.js, node image.test.js).
Created: 2026-10-04. Decisions from review added 2026-10-04.


GOAL
----
A webpage that teaches the Nowak-May spatial games model. It shows the grid
playing the game over time, with a short explanation (a tutorial we will write)
beside it and a few controls for the user. It lives at a link I can share with
friends. Vercel integration is coming soon.


THE MODEL
---------
1. Every square is either a cooperator (C) or a defector (D).

2. When two squares meet they play one round of the prisoner's dilemma.
   Payoff to the first square:

                       vs C     vs D
       I am C           1        0
       I am D           b        0

   - Two cooperators: each gets 1.
   - Defector meeting a cooperator: the defector gets b (b > 1, a parameter);
     the cooperator gets 0.
   - Two defectors: each gets 0.

3. Each square plays that round against its 8 neighbors and sums its points.
   A square does NOT play itself (no self-play).

4. Then every square, all at the same moment, looks at itself and its
   neighbors and copies the strategy of whoever scored highest.
   Then the whole thing repeats.

5. Ties: if the square itself is among the top scorers, it keeps its own
   strategy. Otherwise, if the tied top scorers have different strategies,
   the square becomes a cooperator (C wins ties). Explain this in the tutorial.

6. Edges do not wrap around. Squares on an edge or corner just have fewer
   neighbors (5 on an edge, 3 in a corner).


SETTINGS
--------
- b: slider from 1.00 to 3.00 in steps of 0.01, value shown as a number.
  A change takes effect on the next step.
  b has its own slider only; presets never change it.
  Note from the paper (p. 829): without self-play the "interesting" chaotic
  range is 8/5 < b < 5/3 (1.6 to 1.67), with cooperators near 0.299. (The
  paper's main figures use self-play, where it is 1.8 < b < 2.) Checked in our
  code 2026-10-04 on a random 99x99 start: b = 1.61-1.66 gives ~30% C with
  ~1,700 squares changing per step; b <= 1.59 settles near 75% C; b >= 1.67
  freezes near 7% C. Default b = 1.65.
- Starting position and grid size: the user can choose both. Defaults come
  from the paper. Starting-position presets (famous starts) only set up the
  grid; they do not touch b:
    * Random, 10% defectors, 200x200 (paper Fig. 1 and 2a).
    * Single defector in the center of a 99x99 grid of cooperators
      (paper Fig. 3, the "evolutionary kaleidoscope").
    * More presets to add as we find them (e.g. a small block of C in a sea
      of D).
- Grid size control: fixed choices 49x49, 99x99, 199x199. Each preset sets
  its default size (random start: 199, kaleidoscope: 99; the paper used 200
  for random, but odd sizes keep a true center square), and the user can
  change it after.
- Reset: makes a NEW random start (random grid, 10% defectors) at the
  current grid size.


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
1. All-C grid: an interior square scores 8, an edge square 5, a corner 3.
#####

# Plan: first draft = `spec.txt` for v1 (plus the language rule change)

## Context
The proposal is submitted and staff feedback (Oct 9) asked for no changes. Per
CLAUDE.md ("Spec first"), the first draft is the written plan in `spec.txt`, which
Cameron reads and OKs before any code is written. Cameron chose "spec.txt only" for
this round. He also asked to drop the Python rule: use whatever fits the project
best. The final app must run on the web with nothing to install and has sliders, so
**JavaScript** fits best (it runs in the browser directly; his spatial-games project
used the same setup, with model logic in its own file and node tests). Node v26 is
installed.

## Changes (3 files, no code)

### 1. `CLAUDE.md`: replace the "Code conventions" section
- JavaScript, plain functions, a short `/** ... */` comment on every function.
- Model logic in `web/model.js` (no drawing, no buttons); page code in
  `web/app.js` + `web/index.html`; no build step, no libraries for the model.
- Tests in `web/model.test.js`, run with `node model.test.js` from `web/`,
  using the same `check` / `checkClose` / `checkThrows` helpers as
  `cancer-project-handoff/reference/spatial-games/web/rules.test.js`.
- Expected numbers in tests are worked out by hand, not copied from output.
- Remove the Python / `main.py` lines.

### 2. `spec.txt` (new, top level, same style as the spatial-games spec)
Sections:
- **GOAL**: answer Q1 of `proposal.md`; v1 reproduces the A&D straight line only.
- **THE MODEL (v1)**, with a small drawing of one person's grid and one cell's hits:
  1. A person = a grid of N cells (default 10×10 = 100). Each cell holds a hit
     count 0…r.
  2. Each year, ages 0 to 84, every cell with fewer than r hits gets its next hit
     with probability p (hits come in a fixed order: only the next one can happen).
  3. The first year any cell reaches r hits = the person's age at cancer;
     stop that person. No cancer by 85 → "none".
  4. Run M people (default 20,000); store a table of {person, ageAtCancer or null}.
  5. Rate per 5-year group (0–4 … 80–84) = cases in the group ÷ (people
     cancer-free at the start of the group × 5), i.e. per person-year.
  6. Slope = least-squares line through log(rate) vs log(middle age), skipping
     groups with 0 cases.
  7. A seeded random-number generator, so a run can be repeated exactly.
- **EXACT ANSWER TO COMPARE AGAINST**: with constant p, a cell's hits by age t are
  min(r, Binomial(t, p)), so P(cell done by t) = P(Binomial(t,p) ≥ r) and
  P(person cancer-free at t) = (1 − that)^N. This gives the expected rate per age
  group without simulation.
- **FUNCTIONS** (one idea each, built and tested in this order): `makeRng(seed)`,
  `stepCell(hits, r, p, rand)`, `simulatePerson(N, r, p, rand)`,
  `simulatePopulation(M, N, r, p, seed)`, `ageGroupRates(table)`,
  `logLogSlope(ages, rates)`, `expectedRates(N, r, p)`.
- **HAND CHECKS (must pass)**, each with numbers Cameron can do on paper:
  - p = 0: nobody gets cancer.
  - p = 1, r = 3: every person gets cancer at age 2 (hits in years 0, 1, 2).
  - r = 1, N = 1: the rate is flat (proposal Test Case 3), expected rate = p.
  - `logLogSlope` on rates made from age^3 returns exactly 3.
  - `expectedRates` for a tiny case (N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5, ages 0–4) worked by hand.
  - Simulated rates within a stated tolerance of `expectedRates`.
  - Slope ≈ r − 1 when hits are rare (proposal Test Cases 1 and 4); the spec
    notes that p·85 must be small (for example r = 4, p = 0.002) or the slope
    falls below r − 1 (the saturation bend we already measured).
- **NOT IN v1 (later versions)**: the carcinogen (which hit, how strong, start and
  stop ages: v2, for Q1 and Test Cases 2 and 5), the web page and sliders (v3),
  dividing cells and immune cells.
- **DECISIONS FOR CAMERON** (listed with a recommended default, to be OK'd or
  changed when he reviews the spec): N, M, default r and p, the rate definition
  (start-of-group × 5 vs exact person-years), and the test tolerance.

### 3. `progress-log.md`: append a 2026-10-09 entry
Journal set up, staff feedback with no changes, switched to JavaScript, `spec.txt`
v1 drafted and waiting for Cameron's OK.

## Not doing in this round
No `web/` folder and no code. No commits (Cameron writes the messages; I'll
suggest what changed once he's happy).

## Verification
- Before writing, re-check every number in the hand checks by hand
  (for example p = 1, r = 3 → age 2; N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5 case).
- Cameron reads `spec.txt` and either OKs it or edits the decisions; nothing is
  built until he does.
- `git status` shows only `CLAUDE.md`, `spec.txt` and `progress-log.md` changed.

Use this tool when you are in plan mode and have finished writing your plan to the plan file and are ready for user approval.

## How This Tool Works
- You should have already written your plan to the plan file specified in the plan mode system message
- This tool does NOT take the plan content as a parameter - it will read the plan from the file you wrote
- This tool simply signals that you're done planning and ready for the user to review and approve
- The user will see the contents of your plan file when they review it

## When to Use This Tool
IMPORTANT: Only use this tool when the task requires planning the implementation steps of a task that requires writing code. For research tasks where you're gathering information, searching files, reading files or in general trying to understand the codebase - do NOT use this tool.

## Before Using This Tool
Ensure your plan is complete and unambiguous:
- If you have unresolved questions about requirements or approach, use AskUserQuestion first (in earlier phases)
- Once your plan is finalized, use THIS tool to request approval

from math import comb, log
def pdone(t,r,p): # P(Bin(t,p)>=r), t = number of yearly chances
    return 1-sum(comb(t,k)*p**k*(1-p)**(t-k) for k in range(r))
def rates(N,r,p):
    S=lambda a:(1-pdone(a,r,p))**N   # cancer-free at start of age a (a chances so far)
    out=[]
    for g in range(0,85,5):
        s0,s1=S(g),S(g+5); out.append((g,(s0-s1)/(s0*5), s0-s1))
    return out
def slope(xs,ys):
    lx=[log(x) for x in xs]; ly=[log(y) for y in ys]; n=len(lx)
    mx=sum(lx)/n; my=sum(ly)/n
    return sum((a-mx)*(b-my) for a,b in zip(lx,ly))/sum((a-mx)**2 for a in lx)

# 02-120 final project: a cancer model — working with Cameron

## Who I am

- Cameron, an undergraduate at Carnegie Mellon taking 02-120 Programming for
  Scientists (Python).
- This is my final project. I'm building it with Claude while still understanding
  every line that ends up in it. My last project of this kind was a simulator of
  Nowak & May (1992), "Evolutionary games and spatial chaos", deployed as a teaching
  web page (https://spatial-game.vercel.app/). This one does the same for cancer,
  starting from Hanahan's "Hallmarks of cancer" (Cell, 2026 version).
- `progress-log.md` says where the project stands. Read its latest entry first in
  a new session, and add an entry at the end of each session.
- Background from before this repo existed: `cancer-project-handoff/HANDOFF.md`
  (local only, not committed).

## How I like to work

- **One idea at a time.** Introduce a single concept, function or change, make sure
  I understand it, then move on. Don't bundle several new ideas into one step.
- **Never hand me code I can't verify.** Every piece of code comes with a way for
  me to check it myself:
  - a plain-English explanation of what it does and why,
  - tests that define what "correct" means, including edge cases (use the
    `test-every-function` skill),
  - and the command to run them, with the output shown.
  Explain checks with numbers I can verify by hand, not by reading code back to me.
  If I couldn't explain it back or check it on my own, it's too big a step.
- **Show me pictures.** Draw small images of test cases and simulation steps so I
  can see what a check means.
- **Small, runnable steps.** Each step should leave the program in a state that
  runs, so I can see the effect of the change on its own.
- **Spec first.** Write the plan into `spec.txt` and get my OK before building.
- **Ask before assuming.** If a design choice is mine to make, ask me rather than
  picking silently.
- **Learning over speed.** When I'm learning a new concept, teach it one piece at
  a time and check my understanding (the `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill) instead of
  giving me the finished answer.
- **Check against the source.** Verify model rules and numbers against the paper
  itself. Say so plainly when something was misread.

## Graded work

- Keep checking the project idea against the course project guidelines
  (`course/guidelines.md`, summarizing `course/Project Description F26.pdf`),
  especially when the concept changes. `concept.md` is a working draft and its
  guideline check table should stay current.
- The project must answer a scientific question. A game alone is explicitly not
  accepted; any game layer must serve the question.
- I write commit messages myself, in my own words. Stage changes and suggest
  what changed, but let me write the message.

The proposal and project are graded. Help me think, explain, and quiz me, but the
proposal answers are written in my words.

## Code conventions

- Python, with plain functions, type hints on every function, and a short
  docstring for each.
- `main.py` is the entry point (`def main(): ...` with an
  `if __name__ == "__main__": main()` guard).
- Run code from inside the project folder so relative paths resolve.
- If there is a web front end, keep the model logic in its own file with its own
  tests, separate from drawing and buttons.

CANCER AGE-CURVE SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
============================================
Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.
Created: 2026-10-09.


GOAL
----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.


THE MODEL (v1)
--------------
1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

   In v1 the cells do not affect each other, so the grid shape does not
   matter yet. It matters later, when cells divide and have neighbors.

2. Each year of age a = 0, 1, 2, ..., 84, every cell with fewer than r hits
   gets its NEXT hit with probability p. Hits come in a fixed order: a cell
   with 1 hit can only gain hit #2, never jump to hit #3.

       one cell, r = 3, p = 0.5 (made-up coin flips):

       age:     0     1     2     3     4
       flip:   miss  HIT   miss  HIT   HIT
       hits:    0     1     1     2     3   <- cancer at age 4

3. The first year any cell reaches r hits is the person's age at cancer.
   That person stops there (they are no longer cancer-free). Nobody reaches
   r by the end of age 84 -> age at cancer = none.

4. Simulate M people (default 20,000) and store a table with one row per
   person:  { person: 0, ageAtCancer: 61 },  { person: 1, ageAtCancer: null } ...

5. Cancer rate for each five-year age group (0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84):

       rate = (cases with ageAtCancer in the group)
              / (people still cancer-free at the start of the group x 5)

   This is cases per person-year, the same kind of number as CI5 (pop.csv
   counts person-years). See DECISION 4 for a more exact version.

6. Slope = the least-squares straight line through
   log(rate) vs log(middle age of the group), using the groups from 25-29 to
   80-84 (A&D used 25-74; CI5 goes to 85+). Groups with 0 cases are skipped,
   since log(0) does not exist.

7. Random numbers come from a seeded generator: the same seed gives the exact
   same people every time, so a test can be repeated. (JavaScript's built-in
   Math.random cannot be given a seed.)


THE EXACT ANSWER TO COMPARE AGAINST
-----------------------------------
With no carcinogen, a cell gets one yes/no chance per year, so after t years
its number of hits is min(r, Binomial(t, p)). That gives, with no simulation:

   P(one cell done by t years)  = P(Binomial(t, p) >= r)
   P(person cancer-free after t) = S(t) = (1 - P(cell done by t))^N
   expected rate in a group g..g+4 = (S(g) - S(g+5)) / (S(g) x 5)

The simulation must land close to this (HAND CHECK 6). It is a stronger check
than "slope = r - 1", which is only true when hits are rare.


FUNCTIONS (built and tested one at a time, in this order)
---------------------------------------------------------
  makeRng(seed)                    -> a function giving numbers in [0, 1)
  stepCell(hits, r, p, rand)       -> the cell's hits after one year
  simulatePerson(N, r, p, rand)    -> age at cancer, or null
  simulatePopulation(M, N, r, p, seed) -> the table of people
  ageGroupRates(table)             -> 17 groups: cases, at risk, rate
  logLogSlope(ages, rates)         -> the slope of the straight line
  expectedRates(N, r, p)           -> the exact rates from the formula above


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
All numbers below were worked out by hand and double-checked with a separate
calculation on 2026-10-09.

1. p = 0: nobody ever gets cancer (every ageAtCancer is null).

2. p = 1, r = 3: every cell gains a hit every year (ages 0, 1, 2), so every
   person gets cancer at age 2.

3. r = 1, N = 1 (one hit, proposal Test Case 3): the rate is flat. Each year
   the chance is p, so in every group the rate is (1 - (1 - p)^5) / 5.
   With p = 0.1: (1 - 0.59049) / 5 = 0.081902 in EVERY group.

4. logLogSlope on rates made from rate = age^3 returns exactly 3.
   (Also: rate = age^0 returns 0, and a two-point case worked by hand.)

5. expectedRates for a tiny case, N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5:
   - Group 0-4: after 5 coin flips, P(at least 2 heads) = 1 - 6/32 = 26/32.
     Everyone started cancer-free, so rate = (26/32) / 5 = 0.1625.
   - Group 5-9: cancer-free at 5 = 6/32 = 192/1024. Cancer-free at 10 =
     P(at most 1 head in 10) = 11/1024. Cases = 181/1024.
     Rate = (181/1024) / (192/1024) / 5 = 181/960 = 0.18854.

6. Simulation vs formula: with the default settings, each group's simulated
   case count is within 3 standard deviations (about 3 x sqrt(expected
   count)) of the expected count. See DECISION 5.

7. Slope vs r - 1 (proposal Test Cases 1 and 4): with r = 4, the slope is
   close to 3, but not equal, because hits are not perfectly rare:
     r = 4, p = 0.002 -> exact slope 2.99, but only about 56 cases in
                         20,000 people (too few to measure)
     r = 4, p = 0.005 -> exact slope 2.84, about 1,750 cases  <- default
   The simulated slope must be within 0.15 of the exact slope (2.84), and
   the gap from 3 is explained by the same flattening we measured in the
   tutor session (r = 7, p = 0.05: slopes 4.0 -> 2.6).


DEFAULTS (proposed)
-------------------
  N = 100 cells, r = 4 hits, p = 0.005 per year, M = 20,000 people, seed = 1.
  Work: 20,000 x 100 x 85 = 170 million coin flips, a second or two in node.
  Real cancers are far rarer; p is scaled up so the curve has enough cases
  (proposal Q2). Only the shape of the curve is compared with real data.


NOT IN v1 (later versions)
--------------------------
  v2: the carcinogen. It multiplies p for ONE chosen hit (#1 ... #r) between a
      start age and a stop age. This is what Q1 asks about, and what proposal
      Test Cases 2 (the 5,000x timing check) and 5 (the bend vs CI5) need.
  v3: the web page: sliders for p, which hit, start and stop; the log-log
      graph next to CI5 England lung cancer in men; presets.
  Later: cells that divide (Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002), immune cells.


DECISIONS FOR CAMERON (OK the default, or change it)
----------------------------------------------------
1. Cells per person N: 100 (10 x 10)?
2. People M: 20,000?
3. Default r = 4 and p = 0.005 for the v1 checks? (A&D's real sites need
   r of about 6-7; lung in CI5 England looks like 9. Those come in v2 with
   a scaled-up p.)
4. Rate formula: "cancer-free at start of group x 5" (simple, matches the
   hand checks above) or exact person-years (count each person's years
   cancer-free inside the group; closer to how CI5 counts)?
5. Tolerance: within 3 standard deviations for case counts, and within 0.15
   for the slope?

content.text:
## 1) How many cells

Yes, we found three sources on Oct 7. They're in `research/cell-rules-candidates.md`:

| Source | Cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002 | about 10^8 colon stem cells | confirmed |
| Nicholson et al. 2018 | about 10^7 crypts × about 7 stem cells per crypt ≈ 7×10^7 | confirmed |
| Tomasetti & Vogelstein 2015 | 2×10^8 | not confirmed |

All of these are about the colon. We don't have a lung number yet.

We can't simulate 10^8 cells per person, but in v1 we don't need to. When hits are rare, a person's risk by age t is about N × C(t, r) × p^r. That means N and p trade off against each other:

- **N (number of cells)** only raises or lowers the whole line. It doesn't change the slope.
- **p (chance of a hit per year)** changes the height and also controls the bend.

So 100 cells with p = 0.005 behaves almost like 10^8 cells with p = 0.005 × (100 / 10^8)^(1/4) ≈ 0.00016. We're shrinking the person for speed, and the shape of the curve stays the same.

The paper numbers start to matter in later versions. When cells sit in crypts and divide, Nicholson's 7 stem cells per crypt could set the grid layout.

## 2) Why 20,000 people

There was no real logic. I picked 20,000 as a round number that gives about 1,750 cases and should run fast. Here's a way to choose it properly.

A random count is uncertain by about √(count). For example, if 100 cases are expected, you'll usually get 90–110 (±10%).

The fewest cases come in the youngest group we fit, ages 25–29:

| People | Expected cases at 25–29 | Noise |
|---|---|---|
| 20,000 | about 16 | √16 = 4, so ±25% |
| about 123,000 | 100 | ±10% |

**Rule:** pick the smallest number of people that gives at least 100 expected cases in the 25–29 group. The catch is speed: 123,000 people is about 6× the work. We'll time it when we build `simulatePopulation`. Keeping 20,000 for now is fine.

## 3) Why r = 4 and p = 0.005

**r = 4:** I picked it for the math check, not for biology. Slope 3 is easy to recognize, and a small r runs fast. There are real-data choices for later:
- Armitage & Doll's Table I slopes are 5–6.5, so r = 6–7.
- CI5 England lung cancer in men has a slope of about 8, so r ≈ 9.

**p = 0.005:** this one has some logic, as a trade-off.
- A smaller p gives a slope closer to r − 1 but fewer cases. At p = 0.002 the slope is 2.99, but there are only about 56 cases.
- A larger p gives more cases but more bending. At p = 0.005 there are about 1,750 cases, with a slope of 2.84.

The bend grows with p × age, so a rule could be "the largest p that keeps the exact slope within 0.2 of r − 1." Whatever we pick, the exact formula tells us the right slope.

## 4) The rate formula

The rate means **cases per year spent at risk**. The question is how to count those years. Take the age 60–64 group with 1,000 cancer-free people at age 60, where 50 get cancer during the group:

- **Simple:** assume everyone was at risk all 5 years. That's 1,000 × 5 = 5,000 person-years, so the rate is 50 / 5,000 = 0.0100.
- **Exact person-years:** someone who got cancer at 61 was only at risk for 2 of those years (60 and 61). If the 50 cases average 3 years each, that's 950 × 5 + 50 × 3 = 4,900 person-years, so the rate is 50 / 4,900 = 0.0102.

When cancer is rare, the two barely differ. When it's common, they do. In hand check 3 (one hit, p = 0.1):
- simple gives 0.0819;
- exact person-years gives exactly 0.1000, which is p itself.

The exact count is cleaner and closer to how CI5 counts, so I'd lean that way. Hand check 3 would then become "rate = p".

## 5) The tolerance

The simulation is random, so it never matches the formula exactly. The tolerance is how far off counts as "still correct" before the test fails.

- **3 standard deviations:** if 100 cases are expected, the standard deviation is about √100 = 10, so 70–130 passes. A correct program lands inside this range 99.7% of the time. The cost is that a bug that's off by only 20% could still slip through, so a stricter check (for example ±2.5 standard deviations) is an option.
- **0.15 on the slope:** this was a guess. To set it properly, run the simulation with about 20 different seeds, see how much the slope varies from run to run, and set the tolerance to about 3× that spread.

To redo the spec with these choices, I need two answers from you:
- Exact person-years, or the simple count?
- Should the spec say how we'll pick the number of people and the slope tolerance by measuring them, rather than using fixed guesses?

CANCER AGE-CURVE SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
============================================
Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.
Created: 2026-10-09.


GOAL
----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.


THE MODEL (v1)
--------------
1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

CANCER AGE-CURVE SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
============================================
Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.
Created: 2026-10-09.


GOAL
----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.


THE MODEL (v1)
--------------
1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

   In v1 the cells do not affect each other, so the grid shape does not
   matter yet. It matters later, when cells divide and have neighbors.

2. Each year of age a = 0, 1, 2, ..., 84, every cell with fewer than r hits
   gets its NEXT hit with probability p. Hits come in a fixed order: a cell
   with 1 hit can only gain hit #2, never jump to hit #3.

       one cell, r = 3, p = 0.5 (made-up coin flips):

       age:     0     1     2     3     4
       flip:   miss  HIT   miss  HIT   HIT
       hits:    0     1     1     2     3   <- cancer at age 4

3. The first year any cell reaches r hits is the person's age at cancer.
   That person stops there (they are no longer cancer-free). Nobody reaches
   r by the end of age 84 -> age at cancer = none.

4. Simulate M people (default 20,000) and store a table with one row per
   person:  { person: 0, ageAtCancer: 61 },  { person: 1, ageAtCancer: null } ...

5. Cancer rate for each five-year age group (0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84), using
   exact person-years (decided 2026-10-09):

       rate = (cases with ageAtCancer in the group)
              / (person-years at risk in the group)

   A person adds 1 person-year for each year of age in the group that they
   START cancer-free, including the year they get cancer. Example, group
   60-64: cancer-free all 5 years -> 5; cancer at 61 -> 2 (ages 60 and 61);
   cancer before 60 -> 0.
   This is cases per person-year, like CI5 (pop.csv counts person-years).
   (CI5 divides by everyone alive, including people who already had cancer;
   for a rare cancer the difference is tiny.)

6. Slope = the least-squares straight line through
   log(rate) vs log(middle age of the group), using the groups from 25-29 to
   80-84 (A&D used 25-74; CI5 goes to 85+). Groups with 0 cases are skipped,
   since log(0) does not exist.

7. Random numbers come from a seeded generator: the same seed gives the exact
   same people every time, so a test can be repeated. (JavaScript's built-in
   Math.random cannot be given a seed.)


THE EXACT ANSWER TO COMPARE AGAINST
-----------------------------------
With no carcinogen, a cell gets one yes/no chance per year, so after t years
its number of hits is min(r, Binomial(t, p)). That gives, with no simulation:

   P(one cell done by t years)  = P(Binomial(t, p) >= r)
   P(person cancer-free after t) = S(t) = (1 - P(cell done by t))^N
   expected rate in a group g..g+4 =
       (S(g) - S(g+5)) / (S(g) + S(g+1) + S(g+2) + S(g+3) + S(g+4))
   (top: share of people who get cancer in the group; bottom: expected
   person-years at risk, one year for each age they start cancer-free)

The simulation must land close to this (HAND CHECK 6). It is a stronger check
than "slope = r - 1", which is only true when hits are rare.


FUNCTIONS (built and tested one at a time, in this order)
---------------------------------------------------------
  makeRng(seed)                    -> a function giving numbers in [0, 1)
  stepCell(hits, r, p, rand)       -> the cell's hits after one year
  simulatePerson(N, r, p, rand)    -> age at cancer, or null
  simulatePopulation(M, N, r, p, seed) -> the table of people
  ageGroupRates(table)             -> 17 groups: cases, at risk, rate
  logLogSlope(ages, rates)         -> the slope of the straight line
  expectedRates(N, r, p)           -> the exact rates from the formula above


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
All numbers below were worked out by hand and double-checked with a separate
calculation on 2026-10-09.

1. p = 0: nobody ever gets cancer (every ageAtCancer is null).

2. p = 1, r = 3: every cell gains a hit every year (ages 0, 1, 2), so every
   person gets cancer at age 2.

3. r = 1, N = 1 (one hit, proposal Test Case 3): the rate is flat. Each year
   a cancer-free person has chance p, so cases per person-year = p exactly.
   With p = 0.1: expectedRates gives 0.1 in EVERY group.

4. logLogSlope on rates made from rate = age^3 returns exactly 3.
   Also: a flat rate (age^0) returns 0, and two points, rate 1 at age 10
   and rate 4 at age 20, return log(4) / log(2) = 2.

5. expectedRates for a tiny case, N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5:
   - Group 0-4: after 5 coin flips, P(at least 2 heads) = 1 - 6/32 = 26/32.
